brief: Why most indie founders quit in year 2. The dip nobody warns you about: revenue stalls, burnout, comparison. How to push through to year 3 with AI leverage.

slots.subtitle: The hidden dip between launch and leverage: revenue stalls, burnout peaks, and indie builders quietly quit.
slots.preview1: Why most founders abandon ship by month eighteen
slots.preview2: Three warning signs your runway is becoming a trap
slots.preview3: How AI tools rebuild momentum when motivation dies

slots.title: The Silent
slots.subtitle: Year two is where optimism meets reality and most founders discover they are running on fumes.
slots.insight1Body: Launch revenue dries up faster than projected, leaving no budget for growth experiments.
slots.insight2Body: Solo operators mistake chronic exhaustion for hustle culture and stop measuring health.
slots.insight3Body: Watching peers raise funding or go viral makes disciplined bootstrapping feel like failure.
slots.pullQuote: Year one is a sprint; year two is a marathon nobody trained you to run.

slots.title: When Revenue
slots.subtitle: The plateau after launch month is not a marketing problem; it is a product-ecosystem problem.
slots.insight1Body: Early adopters leave once novelty fades, exposing weak retention mechanics you ignored.
slots.insight2Body: Founders refuse to raise prices because they confuse customer silence with satisfaction.
slots.insight3Body: Relying on a single product line leaves you exposed to platform risk and seasonality.
slots.pullQuote: If your MRR graph looks like a flatline, your business is not broken—your strategy is.

slots.title: Burnout Is
slots.subtitle: Sustainable indie businesses require operators who survive their own ambition without crashing.
slots.insight1Body: Solo founders pile on features because saying no feels harder than shipping widgets.
slots.insight2Body: Without a co-founder or advisor, there is nobody to flag declining decision quality.
slots.insight3Body: Taking a day off crashes progress because no automation exists to cover you.
slots.pullQuote: You cannot optimize a business when the operator is running on corrupted hardware.

slots.title: Comparison Is
slots.subtitle: Measuring your year two against someone else's highlight reel destroys the patience required to win.
slots.insight1Body: Venture-backed growth often hides unit economics that would bankrupt a bootstrapped founder.
slots.insight2Body: A flat MRR month with ninety percent retention beats a viral spike followed by churn.
slots.insight3Body: Indie success is measured in decades, not funding rounds or Product Hunt launches.
slots.pullQuote: The only metric that matters in year two is whether you are still building when others quit.

slots.title: Rebuild With
slots.subtitle: Artificial intelligence is not a replacement for judgment; it is a force multiplier for exhausted founders.
slots.insight1Body: AI agents handling tier-one tickets recover ten hours a week for deep product work.
slots.insight2Body: Code generation and design assistants cut feature development time from weeks to days.
slots.insight3Body: Analytics copilots surface churn signals you would miss while buried in manual spreadsheets.
slots.pullQuote: AI does not save your business; it buys you the time to save it yourself.

slots.title: Make It to
slots.subtitle: Survival is a strategy. The founders who cross the chasm build systems, not just products.
slots.insight1Body: Schedule recovery like a feature release; your capacity is the company's primary asset.
slots.insight2Body: Add a second product, service, or tier before your first stream enters decline.
slots.insight3Body: A small email list of true fans outperforms a massive following of passive scrollers.
slots.pullQuote: Year three belongs to the founders who treated year two as a systems problem, not a motivation problem.

slots.ctaBody: Year two is a filter, not a finish line. Build systems, leverage AI, and outlast the dip.
